sourceLine: your hydraulic hand and industrial results, and the questions line engineers ask before they deploy

cards.title: Cycle Time Is the Production Gate
cards.angle: A wire-insertion task is not production-ready because a robot succeeds once. A line engineer reads success rate and takt together or not at all, and most humanoid announcements publish only the first.
cards.evidence: Your June 2026 proof of concept hit 99.5 percent or better success at a 2.54 second cycle, judged against a Tier 1 supplier's live production benchmarks, on commercial robotic platforms rather than Phoenix. The release states both numbers; the article explains why the second is the harder one and what "matched live-line throughput" required.

cards.title: Zero-Shot Sim-to-Real on a Hydraulic Hand
cards.angle: Teleoperation data is expensive to collect at scale, and a policy trained entirely in simulation shifts part of that cost to compute. Hydraulic actuators are harder to simulate than electric ones, which makes a successful transfer worth more than the demo suggests.
cards.evidence: Your April 2026 demo transferred a sim-only policy to a real hydraulic hand, reorienting a lettered cube ten consecutive times without a drop, after training thousands of hands in parallel in Isaac Lab. What the simulation had to capture well enough for that first transfer to work is the engineering story.

cards.title: What DoF Counts Do Not Tell You About Hands
cards.angle: Degrees of freedom tell a buyer how many motions a hand can command. They say nothing about what it can hold, how it responds to a disturbance, or how it performs after repeated factory cycles.
cards.evidence: Your RL hand work (April 2025) reports in-hand reorientation under a 500 g load not encountered in training, a separate demonstration from the 2026 cube result, and the May 2026 Zeon partnership targets elastomers balancing toughness with tactile precision. The piece sets out the tests a buyer should ask for alongside a spec sheet, without claiming yours win each one.
